options: A compressed copy of the text
A vector representing a text, built so similar meanings point in similar directions
A list of keywords extracted from the text
A hash used to detect duplicates
explanation: It is geometry for meaning: compare vectors instead of text. Cosine similarity between them measures relatedness.

stem: Cosine similarity between two vectors measures…
options: How many words the two texts share
The angle between them, ignoring their lengths
The number of shared dimensions
The Euclidean distance between their endpoints
explanation: Length is deliberately ignored so a long or frequent item does not look 'more similar' to everything.

stem: Why do count-based context vectors put 'cat' and 'dog' close together in the example?
options: The corpus lists them next to each other
They occur in similar contexts, so their rows of neighbouring words look alike
They are both short words
They share letters
explanation: 'Used in similar contexts' becomes 'similar vectors'. Neural embedding models learn a dense version of the same idea.

stem: A retrieved FAQ scored 0.82 similarity to the user's question. What does that tell you?
options: It is the best match among your documents; not that it answers the question
82% of the words match
The threshold for 'correct' has been met
The FAQ answers the question with 82% confidence
explanation: Similarity ranks; it never proves. RAG systems that skip this thought answer confidently from irrelevant context.

stem: Your team moved from one embedding model to another and kept the 0.75 similarity threshold. What should you expect?
options: Only queries in other languages are affected
The threshold is probably wrong now — each model has its own geometry, so re-measure on your data
Scores will be uniformly higher
Nothing changes; cosine is model-independent
explanation: Scores are not comparable across models. Thresholds must be measured per model, and all stored vectors must be regenerated too.

stem: Queries are embedded with model A and documents with model B. What happens?
options: It works if both have the same dimension count
It works because cosine normalises lengths
It only fails for long documents
Vectors do not line up — nearest neighbours are meaningless
explanation: Same model, same version on both sides. Store the model name with the vectors.

stem: 'Reset password' and 'cannot reset password' embed close together. What is the right design response?
options: Raise the similarity threshold
Lowercase the text first
Combine vector search with filters or keyword matching for exact constraints (hybrid search)
Use a longer embedding vector
explanation: Embeddings capture the gist; negation and specifics wash out. Hybrid search (Lesson 6.4) exists for exactly this.

stem: Which of these is NOT typically built on embeddings?
options: Near-duplicate detection
Clustering support tickets by theme
Semantic search
Generating a paragraph of marketing copy
explanation: Generation needs a language model. The other three are nearest-neighbour or clustering over vectors — often with no LLM call at all.

stem: Why embed passages rather than a whole 30-page document as one vector?
options: Long documents exceed the embedding model's dimensions
Whole documents cannot be normalised
One vector averages everything in the document; specific passages stop standing out
Only passages fit in the vector database
explanation: A big chunk embeds the average of many ideas. Chunking (Lesson 6.3) keeps specifics retrievable.

stem: Why should a vector store get the same access controls as the source documents?
options: Vectors contain the raw text
Vectors can be inverted to approximate the original text — they leak content
Because they are usually larger than the documents
Vector databases have no authentication
explanation: Embeddings are not anonymised representations. Treat them as the data they came from.
